name: Cornwall Stone
notes: Matte base glaze with no colorants. Reactive to clay iron — warm yellow-brown over Rod's Bod, whiter and cooler over porcelain. Layers well if not too thick. Lavender uses this base with cobalt as colorant.

name: Celadon
notes: Iron-based celadon — appears red in the bucket. Goes soft blue-grey in reduction; greener in light reduction or oxidation. Crackle is signature. Doesn't combine well with other glazes.

name: Bringle Yellow
notes: Bright glossy yellow. Reactive to clay composition — granny-smith green on iron-rich bodies, optic yellow on porcelain or white stoneware.

name: Blue
notes: Glossy and stable. Reliable true blue. Thin layer under Gitta's Blue creates an oceanic effect.

name: Blue Jean
notes: Chameleonic — sensitive to atmosphere, temperature, and clay body. Sometimes satin, sometimes more glossy.

name: B-18
notes: Built on the same satin base as Black Walnut. Colorant is copper carbonate — extremely reactive to atmosphere and other elements. #18 from a large test batch. Variety of results depending on clay and thickness.

name: Black Walnut
notes: Stable satin base, iron chromate colorant. Taupe on light clays, warmer with speckling on Rod's Bod, near-monochromatic on Dark Brown. Utensil-scuff resistant.

name: Banilla
notes: Warm yellow at times brown. Contains iron, so reacts to base clay. Texturally goes more glossy on higher-shrink clays like porcelain. More brown over iron-rich bodies.

name: Gitta's Blue
notes: Stable turquoise. Layers well, scuff-resistant. Iron in clay body can override its colorants if not mixed thoroughly.

name: Glossy White
notes: Most stable and reliable glaze in the range. Doesn't run, rarely crazes. Opacity varies with dip duration.

name: Pellegreeno
notes: Newer green, similar to the previous studio green but with intensified colorant. Rich and dark on most clays.

name: Green to Black
notes: Textural — at times almost reptilian. Can show warm orangey tones.

name: Lavender
notes: Cornwall Stone base with cobalt colorant. Pale lilac when right; can shift blue. Paler clays bring out more purple.

name: Mottled Blue Cream
application: no more than 4 sec; lip/edge if layering
notes: Rutile glaze. Cloudy taupey to shiny with streaks. Pairs with Pete's Cranberry for mottled effects. WILL run if applied over a whole piece — apply only at lip/edge when layering.

name: Matte Black
notes: Metallic with bronze/silvery crystallization. Many metal colorants flux in reduction — can move on the piece. Use cookies on thick applications.

name: Matte White
notes: Softer, truer matte white than Cornwall Stone. Still shows metals/speckles from clay underneath.

name: Oil Spot
notes: Glossy black with tiny crystallization. Breaks to gorgeous red/brown at edges. Especially nice on angled work.

name: Pete's Cranberry
notes: Classic copper red — rich and deep in good reduction. Studio firing cycle is calibrated to land copper reds. Same colorant (copper carbonate) as B-18, but different flux/base/glass formers produce entirely different results.

name: Ranch Butter
notes: Highest ingredient count in the range. Glossy cream with warming colorants — browns/tans over medium or brown stoneware. Sensitive to thickness — three-prong cracks when dry signal it'll crawl. Caution on filling vessel interiors.

name: Reitz Green
notes: Green to black — bronzey brown-black where thin or breaking. Beautiful green when mixed and applied correctly. Glaze bubbles that crystallize are NOT food safe; refire if it happens.

name: RJ Dry Shino
notes: Shino — occasionally carbon traps. Sensitive to thickness and base clay. The unexpected is the gift.

name: Tangerine
notes: Glossy bright orange, similar profile to Bringle Yellow. Reliable. Brighter on porcelain, earthier on darker stonewares.

name: Toshiko Black
notes: Metallic, glossy, sometimes ashy or silvery. Caution if applying too thick.

name: Transparent
notes: Not truly clear in reduction — no colorant or opacifier, but reduction atmosphere alters it. Thinner = clearer. Pairs with underglazes (apply underglaze OVER the transparent for experimentation).

name: Warm Satin White
notes: Matte/satin counterpart to Ranch Butter. Warm colorant — browns if too thin or over iron clays. Sensitive to thickness; will crawl if over-applied. Smooth, scuff-resistant surface. Watch for cracking while drying.

name: Malcolm Davis Shino
application: vary thickness deliberately; thin areas trap more carbon
notes: The well-known Malcolm Davis carbon-trap shino. Produces oranges, deep reds, and near-blacks depending on application thickness, atmosphere timing, and base clay. Heavy reduction during the carbon-trap window is what produces the dramatic black areas; thinner application reads more orange. Highly variable — the unpredictability is the appeal.

name: Ohata Red
notes: Classic Japanese-style iron-saturated red. Slow cooling encourages crystalline iron development and brings out the rich red — a fast cool can leave it darker/blackish without the red bloom. Distinct from copper reds like Pete's Cranberry: same color family, completely different chemistry. Deeper and more crystalline on iron-bearing clays.
